utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The rest of my questions, General, are very specific, factual questions and shouldn't take very long. I just have a few of them. As Commander of the Zepa operation, who did you report to and when? When you were conducting the Zepa operation, who were you making your reports to and where, when?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were daily reports which were sent to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska for the simple reason that General Mladic designated me to command the units that were engaged towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My next question is: You indicated some visits to your family in the area at the relevant time. I think on July 12th and 13th. When you visited your family or your wife's family, did any discussion come up of these news reports which, we are told by other witnesses, were going on about what was suspected to be happening in the area, to the column and to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 12th, after I went from the Vlasenica command post, I visited my mother, went to visit my mother, and she lives near my wife's family in the village of Leskovac, on the road towards Zepa, further on. And that same night I went to spend the night with my wife's family, and at the time nothing was talked about for the simple reason that nobody knew anything about it. It was between the 12th and 13th of July. Nor was there anything on the information media at all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which they could have heard or that I could have heard. There was nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Given that you were designated, according to your testimony, by General Mladic to take over the Zepa operation on, I believe it was, the night of the 11th - I mean he told you about it; maybe it was the morning of the 12th - did you ever hear from General Mladic why he needed your presence at the Fontana Hotel meetings, if you were to have nothing to do with the evacuation or anything that happened and he wanted you to move on and go on up to Zepa? Why did he say that you needed to come to those meetings at all?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 11th, in the evening, at the Bratunac meeting, I was designated the commander of the forces towards Zepa. I did not know that I would be attending the meeting on the evening of the 11th or the 12th, because he didn't tell me that after the meeting on the evening of the 11th, most probably due to certain reasons concerning General Zivanovic, perhaps, who was there, and on the 12th, wrote the order for the engagement of the buses for the evacuation of the population from Potocari. So probably General Mladic assessed that somebody ought to attend the meeting. Now, whether he gave him the task to go to the command post at Vlasenica and what he was to do there, at the time, on the 11th -- on the evening of the 11th, and 12th in the morning, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You testified, I think, that for some reasonably sizable blocks of time, you were without communication facilities. For instance, from 6.00 to 10.00 on the 12th of July, because the Pribicevac command centre had been disbanded, and then again from the afternoon to the evening of the 12th of July. I'm wondering how could that be. If you were in the middle of getting ready for the Zepa operations, how could you afford to be without communication facilities for any number of hours?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not need any communication facilities because the commanders of the brigades attended the meeting of the 11th, in the evening, at the command headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, and they also heard General Mladic's orders, what they were supposed to do. And on the 12th I went past the units at Viogora, and I saw a number of their commanders and units along the road. I spent a short space of time there and continued on to Vlasenica, to the command post there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But wasn't this the time period when you were just learning about the column moving toward Tuzla, and there was some fear that, in fact, some of the 28th might move in the direction of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier on that there was no assignment of that kind from General Mladic or General Zivanovic that I received. I didn't receive anything like that. And so I didn't consider it to be my responsibility to follow anything in that regard because General Mladic was there, his assistants were there, General Zivanovic was there, they were all there and there was just me, one person who had received an assignment to pull out forces from Srebrenica and the area and to engage them towards Zepa. So that was my prime preoccupation. My sole preoccupation was Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I only have two short questions. One, you mentioned that you did see Kosoric at the Potocari checkpoint briefly on the 12th of July. Did you ask him or did he tell you what he was doing at the Potocari checkpoint on the 12th of July? Did he give you any notion of what was his involvement, if he had any, in the Potocari evacuation, since I believe you said he was fully involved in the Zepa operation as the head of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said something about this previously. He did go with me to pass through Potocari, through Srebrenica, to Pribicevac, and further on to Viogora and towards Vlasenica and Zepa. After I stopped at the Potocari checkpoint, I ordered him to report to me at the forward command post in Krivaca which he did do on the morning of the 13th. As to any information that could have happened at 12 -- on the 12th at noon in Potocari and Vlasenica, he told me nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was Kosoric with you most or all of the time starting when you got to the forward command, for that entire week that you were there, or did he come and go?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you thinking of the Pribicevac or Krivaca forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Wherever you were. I mean, the basis of my question is: Was he close by to you for most or all of that week?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with me the entire time at the forward command post, both at Pribicevac and later on at Krivaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So he was with you all the time during that week. My last question refers to something one of the Defence witnesses said. He said that in the VRS, as in most armies, you have a lot of written rules and regulations, but very often in combat, in emergency situations, those rules and regulations have to go by the board and oral commands take their place. In other words, a person in command may make an oral order that doesn't follow out all of the written requirements that are in the rules. I just want to know if you would agree with that statement, if that's your experience too, that in combat command emergency situations, very often oral orders are given that do away with requirements in the regulations that they be done in writing and have all sorts of technical requirements to them? It's a general question.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An oral order can be issued, especially if it is a short order. But when it was up to me, I never stepped outside the frameworks of what was prescribed by the rules and regulations as to the control and command of the units, the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My very last question has to do with the takeover. I believe you testified that during General Mladic's visit to the Krivaca forward command post on the 15th of the July, he told you that you would be "soon taking over as Corps Commander." At that point did you ask him for further details of when that would happen, or did he offer any, or did he simply say: "Soon you will be taking it over," and you just waited to see what would happen after that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it never burdened me, this taking over of higher duties. The duties I had and the post I had, this was not something that I thought about, nor was I happy to take on any extra duties. I didn't ask him for any explanations. I continued to perform my duties and tasks which emanate specifically in connection to the Zepa operation. Perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. I think perhaps it would be convenient to have a break now, not to begin, since we only have five minutes. So we'll have a quarter of an hour's break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, I will now have a few questions for you. It is true that one is at an advantage when speaking last, but I do have a few questions. You explained at the beginning of your testimony that you followed your education and your career in a multiethnic environment without any hatred or animosity between the various ethnic groups. In that connection, you expressed your surprise when, upon returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, you were able to note that only Serb soldiers were members of the VRS army ranks. My question is the following: In your opinion, what was the objective of this war between the BH and the VRS, specifically?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the ethnic composition of the army of Republika Srpska, I said that my brigade, the one which I took over command of from another commander was monoethnic; however, I know for a fact that many units in the VRS had among their ranks members of other ethnic groups, that is, Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, General Krstic, was this true for 1995 or only for the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in 1995 this was true. In my opinion, I am, in the first place, a career soldier. I have never been a politician, though a General in a certain sense should not get involved in politics but should be familiar with politics. And I said that I found it extremely hard to accept everything that had happened in the area of the former Yugoslavia, and particularly so in the territory of my republic, where I was born and where I grew up in a multiethnic environment. The war in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina was provoked by the policies pursued by all three parties. Why did the war break out? I spoke about that at the beginning. And the person most responsible for all this were the politicians who, in those days, represented all three ethnic groups and all the other ethnicities inhabiting the former territory of the former Yugoslavia. For me, as a person who was born and grew up in a multiethnic community, and especially being an officer who was in command of units that were multiethnic, this was extremely painful, especially when I reached the area and took over control of this command, the members of which were only Serbs at the time. I came voluntarily to the army of Republika Srpska, as did all my colleagues of other ethnic groups who abandoned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm sorry for interrupting you. You said that politics was for politicians, and the war, for Generals, and that the Generals do not determine policies. However, are you aware of the political objectives which you did not determine, but are you aware of the political objectives of that war?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know. I could just think about it. The objective I was aware of was the defence of the people I belonged to, and nothing more than that. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So are you telling me that -- when I'm asking you what was the objective of the war, are you telling me that the objective of the war -- the objective of the VRS was to defend?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to defend who?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war was in full swing already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps we can develop this question on another occasion. You spoke about your return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. When exactly, and I mean what month, did you return to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned in the month of June to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. Did you take the decision to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina on your own personal initiative, or were you obeying an order or following anybody's suggestion in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided on my own accord to return to the place where I was born. And as I said earlier on, I had hoped and was convinced, in fact, that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina would not escalate to the extent it did, but unfortunately that was not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, do you know other military people who were not of such high rank as you, perhaps, other military men originating from Bosnia, Serbs from Bosnia, who remained in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came from the Pristina Corps, that is, from Kosovo, and I testified about that earlier on. I was the most responsible there as the Brigade Commander, in Kosovska Mitrovica, and I couldn't have left until it was -- it collapsed ethnically into its component parts. And then I realised that I had nothing more to do in the army of Yugoslavia, so that I had to go back to where I was born and where I came from. I do not believe that any officer from the Pristina Corps who was born in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of what ethnicity he was, remained in the army of Yugoslavia. So I am not aware of that. In my brigade, not a single officer remained, be he a Serb, a Croat, or a Muslim. Before all these things happened in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, that brigade was a multiethnic brigade, and I can say in all sincerity that as the Brigade Commander, I was proud of that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Krstic, did you know or did you hear reference to an order, maybe it could have been secret, a secret order, dated January 1992, an order by Milosevic to transfer to Bosnia-Herzegovina all JNA officers born in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any such order. All I knew was that once the war had broken out in the former Yugoslavia, first in Slovenia and then in Croatia, that there were transferals of a certain number of officers to the war-swept areas. I cannot say, nor do I know, what ethnic group those officers belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Upon your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were appointed Commander of the Romanija Brigade which you have referred to. What exactly was the area of responsibility of that Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was appointed Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, at the time it was fully engaged on the front lines towards Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares. That was the area of responsibility of that brigade. It's the western part of the Romanija plateau, closer to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any correspondence between this area of responsibility that you have just mentioned and the self-proclaimed autonomous region of Romanija, proclaimed in 1991, and then integrated with the self-proclaimed province of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still in Kosovska Mitrovica, I heard of certain regions being formed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. As for the area of responsibility of my brigade, it has nothing to do with that Romanija province, self-proclaimed Romanija province, because anyway, that is not the same area because Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares do not belong to the Romanija plateau. The Romanija plateau includes the municipalities of Pale, Sokolac, and Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You qualified as short the one-month-long period from the 1st to the 28th of September, when you were transferred from the Commander of the Motorised Brigade of Romanija to the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. You also said that this period of time was fixed in advance. And you also qualified as normal the period of four years that you served as Lieutenant Colonel before becoming promoted to Colonel. Could you tell us how long, generally, it takes to be promoted from the rank of Colonel to the rank of General, in practice?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the rank of Colonel for almost three years after being Lieutenant Colonel. As far as I know, the time it takes to be promoted from Colonel to Major General is not fixed in any way or by any rules and regulations, instructions, orders, or laws. My promotion to the rank of Major General, I do not consider to be anything exceptional because I had served as Colonel for all of three years, and the position of Chief of Staff, according to establishment in the army of Republika Srpska, is held by a Major General. And I was promoted to that rank in May 1995 after returning from treatment at the Military Academy in Belgrade. And before that I was appointed to the position of Chief of Staff of the Corps in 1994, in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a certain point in time, and even today, you said that during the wartime period there were many rules that were not observed. Could it happen, could the same situation occur in relation to the transfer of responsibilities between the former Chief of Staff and the new chief of a corps, a Corps Commander, between the former and a new Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as I know, I didn't say that the rules were not implemented in wartime, at least as far as I am concerned. It was customary in the former Yugoslav People's Army, and later in the army of Republika Srpska, that after one is appointed to a certain position, a process has to take place, a process of takeover duty between the former commander and the new commander that is being appointed to that post. I was appointed to the position of Corps Commander by President Karadzic on the 15th of July, 1995, and the takeover of duty between me and General Zivanovic was carried out on the 20th of July, 1995, on the 20th or the 21st of July, 1995. It was customary at the lower levels of command, lower levels in relation to a corps command, that upon the takeover of duty, the whole ceremony takes place in front of a lined-up unit; however, the corps command is an operational unit and a war was going on which did not allow for such a takeover of duty to take place in a ceremony in front of formally lined-up units. But present at that takeover were the most responsible officers on behalf of the Main Staff, the Commander of the Main Staff, his assistants, and the corps commanders -- some of the corps commanders of the army of Republika Srpska, as well as representatives of the authorities. So that everything was done as prescribed and as was customary in the former army, the Yugoslav People's Army, and in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, General, you explained that when you were in command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, sometimes you would take prisoners of war. What were the centres where these prisoners of war were held in captivity?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke about that. There are two places, when we are talking about the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, where prisoners of war were detained or, rather, where they lived, and those were Knezina, a locality west of Sokolac, in the direction of Olovo; and before that I found the Brigade Commander in Sokolac itself, and the prisoners of war were held in a locality called Cavarine, near Sokolac. So they were in appropriate facilities, in dwelling apartments -- in a building with several apartments. And in Knezina too there was a proper building, which was a building belonging to the agricultural cooperative that used to house the administration of that agricultural cooperative, in that locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was done exactly when prisoners of war were captured, according to your experience?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified about that earlier on. When prisoners are captured, the units that captured the prisoners, and this would usually occur on the front lines, they would report to the Superior Command, that is, the brigade command, and then the Chief of Security or his officer would go to the subordinate unit that carried out the capturing of prisoners, take over those prisoners and bring them to the place where they would be put up or where some war prisoners were already being held in detention. I said that they were treated fully in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and other rules and regulations. They were given the same food as our troops and our officers, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I apologise for interrupting you, but to speed things up a little because we are pressured by time: Did you have any experience with prisoners of war as the Commander of the Drina Corps? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Brigade Commander and as the Chief of Staff or Corps Commander, I did not -- I did not have occasion to have any kind of experience when I held that position [As interpreted]. And I've already said who was responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war. I think I spoke about that at length. Even those prisoners of war that were captured in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik and the 1st Birac Brigade, they were regularly handed over at Batkovici to the centre where they were taken over for exchange, Batkovici being near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a minor remark for the transcript. The General said that as the Brigade Commander he did have experience, but as Chief of Staff and Corps Commander he had no experience with prisoners of war, and I think that the transcript needs to be corrected to that effect. That would be my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is what the General said, except with regard to the Zvornik and Birac Brigades. General, you explained during your testimony that the Chief of Security was an essential component of the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade when you were its Commander. The Chief of Security, did he have a major role in all units and at all levels, be it brigades or corps, or was it something specific to your way of command, or was it specific to that particular brigade? What I mean is, when you say that it is an essential component, does that mean for you personally or in the organisation as a whole?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that as Brigade Commander, for me it was a very important element both in peacetime and wartime with regard to the overall activities of the Security Service, whose main duties are linked to intelligence. So he's an advisory body in any command. And when this is functioning properly, there are no major problems, especially in conditions of war. Let me also add that as Chief of Staff and Corps Commander, and especially as Chief of Staff, I had no occasion to be in charge of the Security Service. In those days I was not the Corps Commander, because the Chief of Security was subordinated to the Corps Commander and to his own Security Service, according to the chain of command, as indicated in the Rules of Service of the Security Organ. Therefore, he is an important link in the counterintelligence activities in any unit. After taking over duty as Corps Commander, and I think I spoke about that too, I simply did not want to have anything to do with that officer, having learnt from my experience with the exceptionally good quality of the work of the head of security in the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade. So how that officer came to have that duty, I don't know. I'm not aware of his qualities. I found him in Vlasenica. And I'm not aware of his qualities as an officer in the Security Service. But I also know that I did have certain problems with him, and the head of the Security Administration, as the Brigade Commander, who had, in a sense, accused me that together with a president of a municipality, I had collaborated with the Muslims while I was Brigade Commander, while I was undergoing treatment at the Military Academy. And in Meljine, they arrested this municipality president. And because of their attitude towards me, that they wanted to get me involved in all that, this dispute between them and me continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, General Krstic, you explained that Colonel Popovic, the head of security of the Drina Corps, was placed under the direct orders of the Commander-in-Chief, that is, of General Mladic. On what date did that take place? Have you any precise idea about that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about that later, when I learnt about all the events that I have mentioned with respect to the prisoners of war of the 28th Division. Most probably the date was the day when the separation started of men in Potocari from their families, the separation of men from their families in Potocari. The officer that I mentioned told me this, that he was -- that he was ordered personally by General Mladic to place -- that he is being placed under the command of Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Krstic, but knowing that the security officer is such an important element and almost an indispensable element, and if General Mladic is appointing you as Commander of the Zepa operation, how do you explain the fact that General Mladic took away from you this officer when he himself had Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Mladic did not take him away from me. He remained in the command in Vlasenica together with the Corps Commander. I did not have a security organ in Zepa all that time. I didn't know where that man was, what he was doing, and under whose orders he was doing what he was doing. I have said I don't know how many times that all my knowledge came much later. Whether General Zivanovic, as Corps Commander, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gave any instructions from the 12th onwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you feel the need for a security officer in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't feel such a need. I didn't feel it. But perhaps it would have been normal for that person to come by occasionally to that area. But I was not the one deciding about that. It was only the Corps Commander, General Zivanovic, who had any authority over him or, according to the chain of command, right up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was there someone who replaced Colonel Popovic in his duties in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, no. He was not at the Pribicevac forward command post even during the Krivaja Operation. He only came on the 11th, as we saw. He arrived in Srebrenica on the 11th. Prior to that, he didn't even visit the forward command post at Pribicevac, which seems to imply that someone else was giving him instructions, the Corps Commander and his superior security department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already spoken today about the checkpoint at Potocari, on the 12th of July, and you admitted that Popovic was with you at that checkpoint; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the meeting ended in the Fontana Hotel, I headed forward and I was followed by the head of the Intelligence Department, Kosoric. I didn't see that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was following us. And when I reached the checkpoint to give that interview, I noticed him. I had no contact with him. I didn't ask him what tasks he had been assigned; I had no right to ask him that, because that was the right that his Corps Commander had or his own Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, General Krstic, do you know where he went from that checkpoint in Potocari? You left. Do you know where Colonel Popovic went?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I had no idea, nor was I interested where he would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point, at that Potocari checkpoint, you gave an interview to the television; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you in a position to grant that interview? And why did the TV choose you, to interview you; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say quite freely that this was a coincidence, that I was the first. They weren't waiting for me, they were waiting for General Mladic and the Corps Commander, or someone else from the civilian authorities from the area. Maybe somebody from the MUP. But I happened to be the first to come along. I gave that interview, but as usual I didn't do it gladly because I don't like to speak to journalists and to appear on television. I simply had no incentive to do that. But they simply came across me. The interview was brief; maybe it took seven or eight minutes in all, as you saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know the journalists, the reporters?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the reporters know you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you aware that in answering the questions of reporters, or in agreeing to give an interview, you could have been seen as one of the major protagonists of the operation against Srebrenica, or at least of implicitly approving that operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never gave the matter any thought, and I don't regret granting that interview, because they introduced themselves as being a crew from Republika Srpska Television. They asked me for an interview, and you are aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we know the interview. Were you in a position to refuse to grant that interview? Could you have refused to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I could have refused to be interviewed, but there was no reason for me to avoid granting that interview since they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that Colonel Popovic was sick after Srebrenica. Can you tell us when he took up his duties again?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really cannot say on what date he took up his duties again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any event, he did go back.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I think this was at the end of August or the beginning of September; I don't know the exact date. But before he came, I had already learnt what I have told you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also explained that you tried to punish Colonel Popovic for his participation in the Srebrenica events. We've already discussed that today. Why did you "choose" - if I might say so in quotation marks - why did you "choose" Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be only one reason: Because he was part of the Corps, and at the time I had learnt only about his involvement, so such an officer had to be removed in accordance with the prevailing conditions at the time. I tried in the way I have described but I did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we know that already. Were there any other persons in the Corps who also took part?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't learn anything to the effect that anyone else from the Drina Corps had taken part in that, especially what he had done together with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can it be said that your source mentioned only Colonel Popovic as having participated in those events?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, and that he used units together with the Security Department of the Main Staff that were not part of the Drina Corps. I was convinced that he was the only one from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to another topic. What was the customary procedure for a transmission of orders coming from the Commander-in-Chief when they have to be carried out by a brigade unit? What is the normal procedure of transmitting such an order, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The customary procedure, if an order is issued from a command post, is for orders to be in writing, with all the necessary parameters that an order needs to contain. However, an order may also be issued orally on the spot if the commanding officer happens to be in the area of responsibility of one of his subordinate units. Oral orders are most frequently brief orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. We have this order of the 14th of September, Prosecution Exhibit 704. Do you remember that order? Perhaps the usher can show General Krstic this order, Exhibit 704. General, should this order have passed through the Corps Commander, then through the Zvornik Brigade Commander, even if the person expected to implement the order, in this case Captain Trpic, was directly named in the order?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is not the order; it's not the right one. Maybe some references have been incorrect. I also see that it is now 3.00 so perhaps we have to make a break, because the questions that I still have cannot be finished by 3.30 or something like that. General Krstic has to go to the hospital tomorrow, I think. Is that so, Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Petrusic? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If we can go into private session, I will explain my reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see we are in public session now. We are going to adjourn for the day. Tomorrow we will have a witness, and when that witness completes his testimony, we will resume my questions for General Krstic. Because I was unable to complete my questions today, I don't have the courage to ask the staff to stay on, so we have adjusted our programme accordingly, that is, in accordance with current needs. We will stop there for today and we will resume tomorrow at 9.30. We wish you a good recovery, General Krstic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of November, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
